name: Aaron Diaz

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Aaron. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for AI companies, employers, unions or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work nights on the surgical ward at the county hospital, mostly people after bowel and hip operations. Night shift starts at eight. I do the ten o'clock drug round, check wound drains and pain scores, help people to the toilet at three in the morning, and try to get the morning bloods done before the day staff arrive. There are two of us nurses and one healthcare assistant for twenty-four beds.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like that nights are calmer and you actually get to talk to people when they can't sleep. One man last week told me his whole life story about running a fishing boat. What wears me out is sleeping in the day with the bin lorries outside, and knowing I'm still slower than the others at spotting when a patient is going off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sounds about right, to be honest. Every year there's a new system that's going to change everything, and then it's just another login.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's what I expected, and that the money should go into staff instead. At work I'd joke that the AI still can't do a three a.m. bed bath. Online I probably wouldn't post anything, I don't really post.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately it changes nothing for me, which is both good and bad. My job's safe, people will always need nurses on nights. But I'm on the lowest point of the pay scale, Lena's a teaching assistant on even less, and I send my mum a hundred a month, so we're always close to the edge.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing my nights, because the night pay is what makes the rent work. I'd keep using the AI app on my phone now and then to quiz myself on drug doses, because that does help a bit. And I'd keep paying my union fees, because pay rises are the only real way out for us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Steady, but a bit flat. Like the next five years are already written and they're not very generous.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said a hundred a month to your mum. What happens if money gets tight?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My mum's rent would come first, honestly, before mine. She cleans offices and her hours got cut last year. Lena and I would eat cheaper and skip the trip to her sister's wedding before I'd stop that money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the first thing you'd do if a pay rise came through?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pay off the eight hundred on the credit card from when the boiler went. Then I'd try to put a bit aside so I'm not panicking every time the car makes a noise.

say: The money should go into **staff**, not another **login** nobody needs.
I'd joke that AI still can't do a **three a.m. bed bath**.
think: My **nursing job** is safe, but our money is always close to the **edge**.
Night pay, Lena's **low wage** and my mum's support leave nothing spare.
do: Keep working **nights** because the night pay covers the **rent**.
Keep using the **AI app** now and then to quiz myself on drug doses.
Keep paying **union fees**, since pay rises are our real way out.
feel: **Steady** but **flat**, as if the next five years are already written.
S0.quote: Every year there's a new system that's going to change everything, and then it's just another login.
fieldNote: His worry is **low pay** and family obligations, not AI.
He already uses AI a little, for **drug-dose quizzes**.
He puts his **mum's rent** ahead of his own comfort.

steps.text: Keep working night shifts on the surgical ward for the night pay
Use the phone AI app to quiz himself on drug doses
Keep paying union fees to back the pay claim

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Thanks. The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That sounds like what's already starting, to be honest. Our discharge letters are half done by a computer already on the day side.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's fine if it gives us more time with patients, and not fine if it's used to cut staff. I'd back the union asking for a rule that every hour saved goes back to the bedside. I'd say that in the staff room, calmly, not on a placard.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I don't think it touches me much on nights, at least at first. Most of what I do is hands-on: drains, turns, pain, getting someone back into bed. The bit that changes is the charting and the handover, and to be honest I'd be glad if a machine did my handover notes at six in the morning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd wait until a couple of the day nurses had used the new charting system, and then I'd learn it properly. I'd ask the practice educator if there's a short course on AI in nursing that the hospital pays for. I'd also keep an eye on the day jobs, because if fewer people want nights I might get extra shifts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly okay. Uneasy about Lena, actually, more than me, because they're talking about AI tutors in schools.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Tell me more about Lena. What does that mean at home?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Lena helps kids with reading in a primary school, one to one. If an app does that, the school might keep the teachers and drop the assistants. Then it's my nights paying everything, and my mum's money, and that doesn't add up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who on the ward would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The ward clerk on days, and the discharge coordinator, because their work is all booking and forms. I'd also worry about the older nurses who hate computers. They're brilliant with patients but they'll get blamed for being slow on the screen.

say: AI is fine if it gives **time back** to patients, not if it **cuts staff**.
Every hour saved should go back to the **bedside**, and I'd back the union on that.
think: My **night work** is mostly hands-on, so it barely touches me at first.
Lena's **teaching assistant** job worries me more than my own.
do: Learn the new **charting system** once a couple of day nurses have tried it.
Ask the **practice educator** about a hospital-paid course on AI in nursing.
Watch for **extra night shifts** if fewer people want them.
feel: Mostly **okay** for himself, **uneasy** about Lena's job.
S1.quote: I'd be glad if a machine did my handover notes at six in the morning.
fieldNote: He waits for **proof** from colleagues before learning a new system.
His household risk sits with Lena's **school job**.
He worries about **older nurses** being blamed for slow screen work.

steps.text: Learn the new charting system after two day nurses have used it
Ask the practice educator for a hospital-paid AI in nursing course
Back the union rule that saved hours go back to the bedside

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's quick. That's before Lena and I have even sorted out whether we can afford a bigger flat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the government needs a plan for people who lose their jobs, and that hospitals mustn't use it as an excuse to run wards on skeleton staff. I'd say it to friends, and I'd probably sign petitions and go to the union rally for once. I'd keep it calm, though, I'm not a shouter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I have about five years: two until the thinking AI is here, three more until the robots. Thinking AI would do my charting and maybe tell the ward when someone's going downhill, which is the bit I'm weakest at. Then from 2031 the robots could do turns and toilets, and a junior night nurse is an easy thing to cut.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start the bachelor's top-up now, part-time, so I'm not stuck with just the diploma. I'd learn the new systems straight away this time, not wait for others. Lena and I would stop saving for the bigger flat and put that money in an emergency pot, and I'd join the union rally.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Not panicking, because there's something to do, but I'd feel it in my chest on the drive home.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You usually wait for others to try things first. Would you really move straight away here?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, because waiting only works when there's time. If AGI comes in two years, the people who wait are the ones left behind. I'd still be careful, but I'd be careful while doing it, not instead of it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you pay for the top-up degree?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The hospital sometimes pays half if you agree to stay two years. I'd take that deal, and Lena's said she'd cover more of the food shop. It would mean no holiday for two years, which we can live with.

say: Government needs a **plan** for people who lose jobs, and hospitals can't run on **skeleton staff**.
I'd sign **petitions** and go to the **union rally**, calmly.
think: I'd have about **five years**: two for thinking AI, three more for robots.
A **junior night nurse** is an easy role to cut once robots can do turns.
do: Start the **bachelor's top-up** part-time now, with the hospital paying half.
Learn new **AI systems** straight away instead of waiting for others.
Move the bigger-flat savings into an **emergency pot**.
feel: **Anxious**, with a tight feeling in his chest on the drive home.
S2.quote: Waiting only works when there's time. If AGI comes in two years, the people who wait are the ones left behind.
fieldNote: The **short timeline** flips his usual habit of waiting for proof.
He sees the **three-year robot gap** as his real working window.
He worries AI will catch the **deteriorating patients** he struggles to spot.

steps.text: Enrol in the part-time bachelor's top-up with half the fees paid
Learn the ward's new AI charting system in the first month
Move the bigger-flat savings into an emergency pot with Lena
Go to the union rally on safe staffing

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. That feels more like a normal plan, at least.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got time, so let's train people properly, with the hospital paying. I'd want the union pushing for a training fund and a promise on night staffing. That's what I'd say in the staff room.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, five years for thinking AI and eight for robots is close to a career change window. I'd be thirty-five when the robots arrive, which is young enough to move. I think I'd be fine if I use the time, and in trouble if I don't.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the top-up degree over three years instead of rushing, so I don't burn out on nights. I'd learn the AI tools once the first wards have them working. And I'd look at the jobs that need a person in the room, like stoma care or pain teams, where you talk people through things.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious but manageable. More like exam nerves than dread.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why stoma care or the pain team?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because those nurses sit with people and teach them how to live with a bag or a new hip. A robot might do the dressing, but someone scared about going home wants a person. I've watched our stoma nurse, Ade, and patients light up when Ade walks in.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you and Lena change at home?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd stay in the small flat for now and save the difference. And we'd talk properly about whether she trains as a full teacher, because that's safer than being an assistant.

say: We have time, so train people **properly**, with the **hospital paying**.
The union should push for a **training fund** and a night-staffing promise.
think: Five years for AI and eight for robots is a **career change window**.
I'd be **thirty-five** when robots arrive, young enough to move.
do: Do the **top-up degree** over three years so nights don't burn me out.
Look at **specialist roles** like stoma care or the pain team.
Stay in the small flat and **save the difference**.
feel: **Anxious** but manageable, like **exam nerves** rather than dread.
S3.quote: A robot might do the dressing, but someone scared about going home wants a person.
fieldNote: He looks for **people-facing** specialist roles as a safe harbour.
He's thinking about Lena **retraining** as a full teacher.
He's still exposed because he's **junior** and his savings are thin.

steps.text: Study the bachelor's top-up over three years alongside night shifts
Shadow the stoma nurse with a view to a specialist role
Stay in the small flat and save the rent difference
Learn the AI tools once the first wards have them running

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And the last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years is a long time in nursing. Half the ward will have changed by then anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty if we use it, and I'd keep pushing the union on training. I wouldn't be one of the people saying it's the end of the world. I'd say it's a change we can plan for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'd feel mostly okay. I'd be thirty-seven when the thinking AI comes, and forty when the robots do, so I'd have had years to get experienced and specialise. Money's still the problem, not the robots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on with nights for now and do the top-up degree when the hospital offers to pay. I'd let the AI tools settle in on other wards first, then learn them. And I'd finally try to build three months of savings, because that's the thing that's always missing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calmer. Uneasy about the money, but I can see a path.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would three months of savings change for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It would mean I could take a course or switch wards without panicking about rent. Right now one bad month and I'm on the credit card. Three months of savings would be freedom, really.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you still worry about Lena in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit, but she'd have time to finish her teaching qualification. I'd say do it now, while the school will still give you time off for it.

say: Ten years is **plenty** if we use it for **training**.
I'd call it a change we can **plan for**, not the end of the world.
think: I'd be **forty** when robots come, after years of getting **experienced**.
**Money**, not robots, is still my real problem.
do: Keep doing **nights** and start the top-up when the hospital pays.
Learn the **AI tools** after other wards have settled them in.
Build **three months** of savings at last.
feel: **Calmer**, still uneasy about money but able to see a **path**.

fieldNote: With ten years, he shifts focus fully to **money** and **savings**.
He keeps his usual **wait-for-proof** approach to new tools.
He encourages Lena to finish her **teaching qualification** now.

steps.text: Keep working surgical night shifts while the old system lasts
Build three months of savings in a separate account
Start the hospital-funded bachelor's top-up degree

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because there's no time and I'm junior with no savings. What would help is the hospital paying for the degree upfront, not half, and some kind of guarantee on night staffing so they can't replace two nurses with one and a robot.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about family. Everybody my age I know is helping a parent somehow. If AI hits our parents' jobs too, the cleaners and the drivers, then my generation is holding up two households on one nursing wage.

headlineQuote: If AI hits our parents' jobs too, the cleaners and the drivers, then my generation is holding up two households on one nursing wage.
portrait: A **27-year-old** junior night nurse on a surgical ward, still slow at spotting a **patient going off**.
He lives with Lena, a **teaching assistant**, and sends his mum a hundred a month.
He usually waits for proof, but a **two-year** warning makes him move straight away.
His real worry across all five pictures is **money**, not the robots.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because he's junior, has no savings, and there's no time.
whatWouldHelp: The hospital paying the **degree upfront**, plus a guarantee on **night staffing**.
